newsitem.title: MACAO: Ramos-Horta says Macau, HK could be Timor guides.
newsitem.headline: Ramos-Horta says Macau, HK could be Timor guides.

text.p: The 1996 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Jose Ramos-Horta said on Monday that the upcoming change of flags in Hong Kong and Macau could point the way to a possible political settlement of the East Timor problem.

Ramos-Horta said the transitions to Hong Kong's handover to Beijing in mid-1997 and Macau's transfer to China in 1999 were both models for East Timor, a former Portuguese colony annexed by Indonesia two decades ago.

"If Indonesia would show all its respect when negotiating with Portugal (over East Timor), as China did when it negotiated with Portugal and England on the transition of Macau and Hong Kong, then this process would be an example to the situation in East Timor," Ramos-Horta said.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting with Macau's governor, General Vasco Rocha Vieira, Ramos-Horta urged Indonesia to reduce its military presence in East Timor, to set free political prisoners and to end torture.

The handovers of Hong Kong and Macau were mapped out in diplomatic negotiations more than a decade ago along lines that should allow them a great degree of political autonomy and the preservation of their capitalist economic systems.
The Nobel laureate paid tribute to the East Timorese resistance movement in exile on his arrival in the Portuguese-administered enclave of Macau on Sunday.
Ramos-Horta, who shared the prize with East Timorese Bishop Carlos Belo, said the award was also a tribute to the Portuguese government for its support for his resistance movement.
Macau offers East Timorese refugees shelter and subsidies, allowing them to work and study in the territory.
Ramos-Horta, who was recently denied a visitor's visa by the Philippines, refrained from criticising that country.
"The Philippines is the most democratic ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) country," he said, adding that he did not want to "complicate things".
The Philippines barred Ramos-Horta from entering last November at the time of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
But Manila said last week Ramos-Horta would be allowed in if the government was consulted in advance. Media reports said the Philippines was afraid of embarrassing its ally Indonesia.

Lisbon quit East Timor in 1975 amid political turmoil in Portugal, and Indonesia invaded the colony and then annexed it in the following year. The United Nations does not recognise Jakarta as ruler of the territory and considers Portugal the administering power.
Lisbon continues to demand self-determination for East Timor through a United Nations-supervised referendum on independence.

Ramos-Horta will be in Hong Kong on Tuesday to give a lecture at the Foreign Correspondents' Club on East Timor and on democracy in Southeast Asia. He will then return to Australia, his country of exile.
Ramos-Horta is the international spokesman for the National Resistance Council, which opposes Jakarta's annexation.
